summary: Verbal aptitude supplies roughly four of the ten General Aptitude questions: a sentence with a blank, a grammar or usage check, an idiom or analogy, and a short passage that asks what follows from it. Each one tests English as it is used in context. Subject-verb agreement, tense and conditional patterns cover most grammar items. Contrast words and connotation settle most blanks. Reading questions reward strict inference: pick the option the text supports without outside assumptions and without extreme wording.
highYield: A blank after a contrast word (despite, although, however, yet): first fix the polarity the blank needs, then pick the word that fits grammatically.
Subject-verb agreement with a long phrase between subject and verb, with each/every/either/neither, and with the proximity rule for either…or and neither…nor.
Inference questions on a 4–6 line passage: the right option restates a limited claim from the text; options with always/never/all or outside facts are lures.
Conditional and tense pairing: if + past perfect needs would have + V3; if + simple past needs would + V1.
Jumbled sentences: find the opener that introduces the subject, then chain pronouns and connectors (however, as a result) to their referents.

topics.title: Tenses and active/passive voice
points: English has 12 tense forms: simple, continuous, perfect and perfect continuous, each in three times. Simple marks a fact or routine (I code), continuous an action in progress (I am coding), perfect a past action linked to now (I have coded), perfect continuous a duration up to now (I have been coding for hours).

Time markers pin the tense: since/for with a duration that runs up to now needs the present perfect or present perfect continuous (She has worked here since Monday); yesterday or ago needs the simple past (She joined two years ago, never has joined two years ago).
Stative verbs (know, believe, belong, own, prefer, seem) describe states and do not normally take continuous forms: I know the answer, not I am knowing the answer.

Passive voice is be + V3, with be carrying the tense: The bug is fixed / was fixed / has been fixed / will be fixed. The object of the active sentence becomes the subject, so the verb agrees with that new subject.
In a sentence with two past actions, the earlier one takes the past perfect: By the time we arrived, the train had left.

In clauses of time and condition (when, after, as soon as, until, if) the simple present stands for the future: I will call you when I reach, not when I will reach. It is high time takes the simple past: It is high time we left.

lesson.why: A tense blank turns on one question: which event happened first, or does the time word fix the form? Reading that correctly settles most tense questions in seconds.
lesson.intro: A verb has a form that tells the reader when something happened. Simple past, such as 'finished', reports an event at a past moment. Past perfect, such as 'had finished', is the same verb with 'had' in front, and it marks an event that happened before another past event. A sentence that tells two past events in the order they happened needs no special form at all; the special form is for the event that came first.

definitions.meaning: The plain past form of a verb, used for an event that happened at a past time: she left.
'Had' plus the past participle, used for an event that was already over before another past event: she had left.
A form in which the subject receives the action, built as 'be' plus the past participle: the report was submitted.

principle.text: Place the events on a time line. In a past narrative the later event takes the simple past, and an event that came earlier than it takes the past perfect. Words such as 'after' and 'before' say which event is first, so a clause they introduce needs no extra marker.

lesson.limits: 'Had' is optional only on the earlier clause, the one introduced by 'after' or 'before'. The later main verb always stays in the simple past: 'After the chief returned, he wished', never 'he had wished'. Stative verbs such as know or own do not take the continuous form, so 'was knowing' is never the answer. Passive voice, which is 'be' plus the past participle ('the bridge was built'), is used when the doer is unknown or unimportant; the tense is carried by 'be'.

example.problem: Fill the blank: By the time the technician arrived, the server ______ already crashed.
steps: Two past events appear: the server crashed, and the technician arrived.
'By the time' with 'already' says the crash was over before the arrival, so the crash is the earlier event.
The earlier event takes the past perfect: had + crashed.
example.result: The server had already crashed; the arrival stays in the simple past.

misconceptions: Using 'had' whenever a sentence is about the past. The past perfect is only for an event that is earlier than another past event; a lone past event takes the simple past.
Thinking a progressive form such as 'was wishing' is more polite or more correct. Verbs of wanting and knowing describe states and normally stay in the simple form.

recall.q: When is the past perfect needed?
recall.a: When one past event was already complete before another past event, and the sentence must show which came first.

recall.q: Which verbs do not take the continuous form?
recall.a: Stative verbs such as know or own, so 'was knowing' is never the answer.

recall.q: What does a time word such as 'after' or 'before' do to the choice of tense?
recall.a: It states the order of the two events, so the simple past is enough for both.

practice.stem: Choose the correct form: After the committee ______ the proposal, the team began the work.
practice.explanation: 'After' already shows that the approval came first and the work second, so the story is told in the simple past: approved. 'Had been approving' tempts because it sounds like an earlier event, but a one-time approval is not a continuing activity. 'Approves' and 'will approve' do not match the past 'began'.

lesson.summary: Put the events in order on a time line: the later event takes the simple past, the earlier one the past perfect, and a time word that already states the order removes the need for extra marking.

topics.title: Subject-verb agreement
points: Phrases added with as well as, along with, together with or in addition to leave the subject's number unchanged: The manager, along with his assistants, was present. Uncountable nouns ending in s take singular verbs: The news is good; Mathematics is hard.

Find the true subject before matching the verb: in The box of expensive chocolates was stolen, the subject is box, so was is right; the phrase of expensive chocolates is a distraction placed between subject and verb.
Each, every, either, neither (used alone), anyone, everyone, someone and one of … take singular verbs: Every one of the computers is functioning; One of my friends lives in Pune.

Collective nouns (team, jury, committee) take a singular verb when the group acts as one unit (The committee has published its report). A plural verb is used when members act separately, mainly in British usage (The jury are arguing among themselves).
With either…or and neither…nor the verb agrees with the nearer subject: Neither the manager nor the employees are aware; Neither the employees nor the manager is aware.
In inverted sentences the subject follows the verb: There are three bugs in the module; On the table lies a stack of reports (the subject is stack, so lies is singular).

lesson.why: Agreement questions test whether you find the real subject. The writer of the question hides it behind a phrase or a list, and the verb must still match it.
lesson.intro: In a sentence the verb has to match its subject in number. In the present tense a singular subject takes a verb ending in -s ('the file opens') and a plural subject does not ('the files open'). The subject is the main noun doing the action or being described. Words that follow a preposition such as 'of', 'on' or 'in' describe the subject but are not the subject, so they cannot change the verb.

definitions.meaning: The noun or pronoun that the sentence is about and that the verb must agree with.
Extra words, often starting with a preposition, that describe a noun without becoming the subject.

principle.text: Cross out every modifier phrase, find the head noun that is left, decide whether it is singular or plural, and give the verb that number. A list of items after a colon or a dash is the content of the sentence, not its subject.

lesson.limits: Order can hide the subject: in 'There is a bug', the subject comes after the verb. Either/or and neither/nor follow the nearer subject, and collective nouns can be singular or plural depending on whether the group acts as one unit, so the first noun is not always the one to match. A list introduced by 'as follows' also needs the phrasal verb 'break down', which means 'be itemised': match the number first ('breaks' for a singular total), then keep the particle 'down', because 'breaks' alone does not mean itemised.

example.problem: Choose the verb: The list of pending tickets (is / are) on the board.
steps: Cross out the modifier phrase 'of pending tickets'.
What is left is 'the list', a singular noun.
The singular subject takes the singular verb 'is'; 'tickets' is plural but belongs to the modifier.
example.result: The list of pending tickets is on the board.

misconceptions: Matching the verb to the noun nearest to it. In 'The box of chocolates was stolen' the nearest noun is 'chocolates', but the subject is 'box'.
Treating 'along with' like 'and'. 'The manager, along with her team, was present' keeps a singular subject, because 'along with' adds a modifier and not a second subject.

recall.q: How do you find the true subject of a sentence?
recall.a: Remove modifier phrases such as 'of ...' and 'along with ...'; the head noun that remains is the subject.

recall.q: Do 'each' and 'every one of' take a singular or plural verb?
recall.a: A singular verb: each of the computers is working.

recall.q: With 'neither ... nor', which subject does the verb match?
recall.a: The nearer one, the noun that comes right before the verb.

options: The cost of the new servers are rising.
The cost of the new servers is rising.
The costs of the new server is rising.
The cost of the new servers were rising.
practice.explanation: The subject is 'cost', which is singular, so the verb is 'is'. The first option tempts because 'servers' sits right before the verb. The third mismatches the plural 'costs' with 'is', and the last uses the plural verb 'were' with the singular subject 'cost'.

lesson.summary: Strip the modifier phrases, find the head noun, and match the verb to its number; a list or a phrase after the subject never changes it.

topics.title: Articles and prepositions
points: The choice between a and an depends on the first sound, not the first letter: a university, a one-time fee, a European (all begin with a consonant sound); an hour, an honest official, an MBA (all begin with a vowel sound).

The is used for a specific or already mentioned noun, for superlatives (the fastest algorithm), for unique things (the sun) and for ordinals (the first step). Uncountable nouns in a general sense take no article: Information is power, not An information is power.
Prepositions of time: in for months, years, seasons and centuries (in May, in 2027); on for days and dates (on Monday, on 5 June); at for clock times and points (at 10 a.m., at noon, at night).

Prepositions of place and direction: at a point (at the gate), in an enclosed space (in the lab), on a surface (on the desk); into and onto mark movement; between is for two items and among for three or more.

Some words fix their preposition: senior to, junior to, superior to and prefer A to B (never than); comply with, capable of, insist on, interested in. Phrasal verbs change meaning with the particle: put off (postpone), put up with (tolerate), call off (cancel).

No article before languages, meals, games and most proper names (She speaks French; after lunch; he plays chess), but the before rivers, oceans, mountain ranges, newspapers and plural country names (the Ganga, the Himalayas, the Netherlands).

lesson.why: A single blank often asks for 'a' or 'an', or for 'for' or 'since'. These rules are short, and a learner who knows them answers by rule instead of by feel.
lesson.intro: The articles are 'a', 'an' and 'the'. 'A' and 'an' point to one unspecified thing; 'the' points to one particular thing both speaker and listener already know. A preposition is a small word, such as 'in', 'on', 'for' or 'since', that links a noun to the rest of the sentence and often tells time or place. Each of these small words has its own job, and choosing between them is a matter of the rule for that job.

definitions.meaning: 'A' or 'an', which introduce one unspecified member of a class.
A word such as for, since, in, on or at that ties an event to a length of time or a moment.

principle.text: Use 'a' before a consonant sound and 'an' before a vowel sound, judged by pronunciation and not by spelling. For is followed by a length of time (for three weeks); since is followed by a starting point (since Monday).

lesson.limits: The a/an rule is about sound, so 'a university' and 'an hour' break the spelling rule. Some words fix their own preposition (prefer A to B, senior to, comply with), and these must be learned as fixed pairs because no general rule predicts them. Within plus a length sets a deadline (finish within two days), while during takes a named period or event (during the exam) and not a bare count.

example.problem: Fill the blanks: She has been working on the compiler ______ four days, ______ Monday morning.
steps: 'Four days' is a length of time, so the first blank takes 'for'.
'Monday morning' is a point where the work began, so the second blank takes 'since'.
Do not swap them: 'since four days' puts a length after 'since'.
example.result: for four days, since Monday morning

misconceptions: Choosing 'an' for every word that starts with a vowel letter. 'University' starts with the sound 'yoo', a consonant sound, so it takes 'a'.
Treating 'for' and 'since' as interchangeable. A length takes 'for' and a starting point takes 'since'; mixing them is always an error.

recall.q: How do you choose between 'a' and 'an'?
recall.a: By the first sound of the next word: 'an' before a vowel sound, 'a' before a consonant sound.

recall.q: Which preposition goes with a point in time, 'for' or 'since'?
recall.a: 'Since' takes the point where something began; 'for' takes a length of time.

recall.q: Which preposition follows 'prefer' in 'prefer tea ___ coffee'?
recall.a: 'To', never 'than'.

options: He is an European student at a honest institute.
He is a European student at a honest institute.
He is a European student at an honourable institute.
He is an European student at an honourable institute.
practice.explanation: 'European' begins with the sound 'yoor', a consonant sound, so it takes 'a'. 'Honourable' begins with a silent h and the vowel sound 'on', so it takes 'an'. Option 1 tempts because its first half is right, but 'a honest' is wrong: honest also has a silent h, so it needs 'an'. Options 0 and 3 tempt by following the spelling: 'an European' treats the letter and not the sound, and option 0 repeats that fault in 'a honest'.

lesson.summary: A/an follows the sound of the next word, and for, since, in, on and at each have one job; learn the fixed pairs, since no rule predicts them.

topics.title: Conjunctions, correlatives and parallel structure
points: Coordinating conjunctions (FANBOYS: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so) join units of equal rank. Subordinating conjunctions (because, although, unless, while, since) attach a dependent clause to a main clause.
Correlative pairs must be complete and correctly matched: either…or, neither…nor, not only…but also, both…and, whether…or. Mixing them, as in neither…or or both…as well as, is an error.
The two halves of a correlative must be grammatically parallel: She is not only skilled but also patient (adjective, adjective), not She not only is skilled but also patient.
Although and but should not be used together in the same sentence; one contrast marker is enough: Although it rained, the match continued, not Although it rained, but the match continued.
Items in a list keep one grammatical form: He likes coding, testing and debugging, not He likes coding, to test and debugging.

Hardly, scarcely and barely pair with when, and no sooner pairs with than; placed first, they invert the verb: No sooner had the bell rung than the students left; Hardly had I sat down when the phone rang. Lest takes should or the base verb: Walk carefully lest you fall.

lesson.why: Correlative pairs and list items are a favourite grammar check: the wrong option usually breaks a pair or mixes forms, and you can spot both by looking at the words around the blank.
lesson.intro: A conjunction is a small word that joins two parts of a sentence. Some, like "and" or "but", join parts of equal weight. Others, like "because" or "although", attach a smaller clause to the main one. Some conjunctions come as a fixed pair, such as "either ... or"; both halves must appear, and the words that follow each half must be the same kind of word. That matching of kinds is called parallelism.

definitions.meaning: One of for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so (FANBOYS); it joins two units of equal rank.
A fixed pair such as either...or, neither...nor, not only...but also, both...and, whether...or.
Giving joined or listed items the same grammatical form, such as all nouns or all gerunds.

principle.text: Use each correlative with its own partner, and put the same kind of phrase after both halves. In a list, every item takes one form. One contrast marker is enough in a sentence, and "no sooner" pairs with "than" while "hardly" and "scarcely" pair with "when".
principle.tex: \text{either } X \text{ or } Y,\quad \text{not only } X \text{ but also } Y \qquad X, Y \text{ same form}

lesson.limits: Parallelism concerns grammatical form, not length: "tall and very intelligent" is fine because both are adjectives. Nothing here fixes which verb agrees with the subject after neither...nor; that is a separate agreement rule.

example.problem: Choose the correct option: She is not only skilled ______ patient. (a) and also  (b) but also  (c) as well as  (d) or also
steps: "Not only" is the first half of a correlative, so we need its own partner.
The partner of "not only" is "but also", which rules out "and also", "as well as" and "or also".
Check parallelism: "skilled" and "patient" are both adjectives, so the form matches.
example.result: She is not only skilled but also patient.

misconceptions: Treating any two joining words as interchangeable. "Neither...or" and "both...as well as" are broken pairs even though each word is real.
Writing "Although it rained, but the match went on". Although already marks the contrast, so "but" is a second marker and the sentence is wrong.

recall.q: Which word completes the pair "no sooner"?
recall.a: "Than": No sooner had the bell rung than the students left.

recall.q: What does parallelism ask of a list of items?
recall.a: Every item has the same grammatical form, for example coding, testing and debugging, all gerunds.

recall.q: What follows "hardly" or "scarcely" when it starts a sentence?
recall.a: The verb is inverted and the second clause begins with "when": Hardly had I sat down when the phone rang.

practice.stem: Choose the sentence that is grammatically correct.
options: He enjoys swimming, to cycle and running.
He enjoys swimming, cycling and running.
He enjoys to swim, cycling and running.
He enjoys swimming, cycling and to run.
practice.explanation: The list needs one form throughout, and swimming, cycling and running are all gerunds. Each other option mixes a gerund with an infinitive, which tempts because every item is a real verb form and the sentence still sounds fluent.

lesson.summary: Pair each correlative with its own partner, give joined items one grammatical form, use a single contrast marker, and remember that no sooner takes than while hardly and scarcely take when.

topics.title: Adjectives, adverbs, comparison and modifiers
points: Degrees of comparison: positive (fast), comparative (faster than, more efficient than) and superlative (the fastest, the most efficient). Never double them: more faster and most fastest are errors.
Fewer goes with countable nouns and less with uncountable ones: fewer bugs, fewer drops, but less water, less time. Many/much and number/amount follow the same countable/uncountable split.
A modifier must sit next to the word it describes. A misplaced modifier attaches to the wrong word: He served sandwiches to the guests on paper plates suggests the guests sat on the plates.
A dangling modifier has no doer in the main clause: Walking to the station, the rain began. The opening phrase needs its doer as the subject: Walking to the station, I got caught in the rain.

Adjectives qualify nouns and adverbs qualify verbs, adjectives or other adverbs: She sings beautifully, not She sings beautiful. Linking verbs (feel, look, seem) take adjectives: The food tastes good.

Stacked adjectives follow the order opinion, size, age, shape, colour, origin, material, purpose, then the noun: a lovely small old Italian wooden dining table. Irregular comparisons: good, better, best; bad, worse, worst; little, less, least. Compare like with like: higher than that of a teacher.

lesson.why: Comparison blanks look easy, yet the options differ by one doubled word or one misplaced word. Knowing the frames removes the guessing.
lesson.intro: An adjective describes a noun ('a fast car') and an adverb describes a verb, an adjective or another adverb ('she drives fast'). To compare, English has set frames: 'as ... as' says two things are equal, a word ending in -er followed by 'than' says one is greater, and the -est form says one is greatest of a group. The word between the two 'as' is always in its plain form.

definitions.meaning: The plain form of an adjective or adverb, such as good or well.
The form that compares two things, such as better or more efficient, used with 'than'.

principle.text: Equality uses the frame 'as + plain word + as'. The frame already carries the comparison, so the word inside takes no -er, -est, 'more' or 'most'. 'Enough' comes after an adjective or adverb ('bright enough') and before a noun ('enough water').

lesson.limits: The plain-form rule holds only for equality. In a 'than' comparison the comparative is required, and the two things compared must be alike: compare 'her salary' with 'his salary' or 'his', not with 'him'. Good is an adjective and well is an adverb, though 'well' is also an adjective for health.

example.problem: Fill the blank: Mina can solve the puzzle ______ her brother. Options: (a) as better as (b) as well as (c) as best as (d) as good as.
steps: Every option sits inside an 'as ... as' frame, which is the equality frame, so the word between the two 'as' must be a plain form. (a) and (c) put a comparative and a superlative inside it, so both go.
The word describes how she solves, which makes it an adverb, and the adverb of 'good' is 'well'.
(d) keeps the frame but uses the adjective 'good' where an adverb is needed.
example.result: Mina can solve the puzzle as well as her brother.

misconceptions: Writing 'as better as' to sound stronger. The frame already compares, so a second comparison inside it is wrong.
Placing 'enough' before the adjective, as in 'enough bright'. With an adjective, 'enough' follows it: 'bright enough'.

recall.q: What form sits between the two 'as' in an equal comparison?
recall.a: The plain form, such as well, tall or fast, with no -er, -est, more or most.

recall.q: Where does 'enough' go with an adjective?
recall.a: After it: 'bright enough to be seen'.

recall.q: In a 'than' comparison, what must be true of the two things compared?
recall.a: They must be alike: compare 'her salary' with 'his', not with 'him'.

options: The server is enough fast to handle the load.
The server is as faster as the old one.
The server is fast enough to handle the load.
The server is as fast enough as the old one.
practice.explanation: 'Enough' follows the adjective: 'fast enough to handle'. The first option tempts because 'enough fast' sounds natural in speech but puts 'enough' in front. The second and fourth add a comparative or 'enough' inside the 'as ... as' frame, which must hold only a plain form.

lesson.summary: Equality is 'as + plain word + as', 'enough' follows an adjective, and a second comparison inside a comparison frame is always an error.

topics.title: Pronouns: antecedents, case, reflexives and relatives
points: A pronoun agrees with its antecedent in number and gender, and the antecedent must be clear: Each student must bring his or her own laptop. When two nouns could be meant, as in Ravi told Amit that he had won, rewrite with a name.
Case follows the role in the clause: subject forms (I, he, who) for subjects and object forms (me, him, whom) after verbs and prepositions. Between you and me is correct; between you and I is not.

Reflexive pronouns (myself, themselves) are used only when the subject acts on itself or for emphasis: She taught herself Python. Using them in place of I or me, as in Please contact myself, is an error.

Relative pronouns: who/whom for people, which for things, whose for possession and that for restrictive clauses. A quick test: use whom when the answer would be him (Whom did you invite? You invited him).
Its is possessive and it's means it is or it has: The committee announced its decision; It's time to vote.

A relative pronoun takes the number of its antecedent: She is one of the engineers who have cleared the test (who refers to engineers, plural), but She is the only one of the engineers who has cleared it (who refers to the only one).

lesson.why: Pronoun questions ask two things in one: does the pronoun agree with its noun, and could the reader tell which noun it means? A sentence can be grammatical and still be unclear.
lesson.intro: A pronoun is a short word, such as 'he', 'it' or 'they', that stands in for a noun mentioned earlier. The noun it replaces is called its antecedent. A pronoun is only useful if the reader can tell which noun it replaces. If two earlier nouns could both be the antecedent, the sentence is ambiguous, even if every word is correct.

definitions.meaning: The earlier noun that a pronoun refers back to.
A pronoun that could stand for two or more earlier nouns, so its meaning is not fixed.

principle.text: A pronoun agrees with its antecedent in number and gender, and it must have exactly one possible antecedent. Indefinite pronouns such as everybody, each and someone are singular and take singular verbs. If a reader could pick two nouns, the sentence is ambiguous.

lesson.limits: Agreement can be perfect and the sentence still ambiguous: 'Ravi told Amit that he had won' has two valid readings. A pronoun with only one possible noun of its gender and number, as in 'Meera told Amit that she had won', is clear.

example.problem: Is this sentence clear? 'Priya met Neha after she got the offer letter.'
steps: The pronoun 'she' follows two nouns, Priya and Neha.
Both are female and singular, so either could be the antecedent.
Reading one: Priya got the letter. Reading two: Neha got the letter. The reader cannot choose.
example.result: The sentence is ambiguous; repeating a name fixes it: 'after Neha got the offer letter'.

misconceptions: Treating 'everybody' as plural because it names many people. It is grammatically singular: 'Everybody is ready'.
Believing a grammatically correct sentence is automatically unambiguous. Agreement and clear reference are separate tests.

recall.q: What is an antecedent?
recall.a: The earlier noun that a pronoun stands for.

recall.q: When is a pronoun reference ambiguous?
recall.a: When two or more earlier nouns of matching number and gender could be the one the pronoun means.

recall.q: Is 'each of the students' singular or plural?
recall.a: Singular, so it takes 'is' and 'his or her': each of the students has submitted.

practice.stem: Read the sentence: 'Kavya told Isha that she had passed.' Which observation is correct?
options: It is unambiguous, because both names are female.
It is ambiguous, because 'she' could mean Kavya or Isha.
It is ungrammatical, because 'she' should be 'her'.
It is unambiguous, because the first noun is always the antecedent.
practice.explanation: Both Kavya and Isha are singular and female, so 'she' fits either, and the sentence has two readings. The first option tempts by confusing matching gender with clarity, when matching gender is exactly what makes the reference unclear. 'She' is correctly the subject of 'had passed', and no rule makes the first noun the antecedent.

lesson.summary: A pronoun needs one clear antecedent and must agree with it; indefinite pronouns are singular, and two possible antecedents make a sentence ambiguous.

topics.title: Conditionals and reported speech
points: Zero conditional states a general truth with present + present: If you heat ice, it melts. First conditional states a real future possibility with present + will: If it rains, I will stay home.

Second conditional imagines an unreal present with simple past + would + V1: If I had a million rupees, I would travel. With be, formal usage takes were for every person: If I were you, I would accept the offer.
Third conditional imagines an unreal past with past perfect + would have + V3: If I had studied, I would have passed. Would have in the if-clause (If I would have studied) is always wrong.

In reported speech after a past reporting verb, tenses shift back one step: present to past, past and present perfect to past perfect, will to would, can to could. Time and place words shift too: tomorrow becomes the next day, here becomes there, now becomes then.

Reported questions take statement word order and drop the question mark: He asked, "Where do you live?" becomes He asked where I lived. Yes/no questions take if or whether. Commands become to + V1: She told me to close the door.

lesson.why: Conditional sentences and reported speech are tested through verb forms, so knowing the fixed pattern for each type lets you pick the right option without re-reading the whole sentence.
lesson.intro: A conditional sentence has an "if" part, which states a condition, and a result part. The verb forms in the two parts change with how real the condition is: a general fact, a real possibility, an imagined present, or an imagined past. Reported speech retells what someone said without quoting. When the retelling is set in the past, the verbs move one step back in time, and words like "tomorrow" or "here" change too.

definitions.meaning: If + present, will + base verb; a real possibility in the future.
If + simple past, would + base verb; an unreal situation in the present.
If + had + past participle, would have + past participle; an unreal situation in the past.
The move of each verb one step back in time when speech is reported after a past verb such as said.

principle.text: Match the if-clause and result clause to the type of condition. In reported speech after a past reporting verb, shift present to past, past to past perfect and will to would, change time and place words, and use statement word order in reported questions.

lesson.limits: A universal truth may keep its tense when reported: He said that water boils at 100 degrees Celsius. Backshift is not needed when the reporting verb is in the present, as in "He says that he is tired". "Would have" never goes in the if-clause.

example.problem: Report this: He asked, "Where do you live?"
steps: "Asked" is past, so the verb "live" in the question moves back to the past: lived.
A reported question uses statement order and no question mark, so "do you live" becomes "I lived" after the question word.
The pronoun "you" now refers to the person being told, so it becomes "I" here.

misconceptions: Writing "If I would have studied, I would have passed". Would have belongs only in the result clause; the if-clause takes had + past participle.
Keeping the question order when reporting a question, as in "He asked where did I live". Reported questions use statement order.

recall.q: Which pattern forms the second conditional?
recall.a: If + simple past, would + base verb, as in If I had a million rupees, I would travel.

recall.q: What happens to "will" and "can" in backshift?
recall.a: They become "would" and "could" when the reporting verb is in the past.

recall.q: How is a reported yes/no question introduced?
recall.a: With "if" or "whether", followed by statement word order and no question mark.

practice.stem: Choose the correct sentence about an unreal past event: ______ earlier, we would have caught the train.
practice.explanation: An unreal past event takes the third conditional, so the if-clause needs had + past participle: had left. "If we left" tempts because it is a plain past form, but it expresses an unreal present, not a past that did not happen. "Would leave" is never used in the if-clause.

lesson.summary: Choose the verb pattern by the type of condition, never put would have in the if-clause, and when reporting speech after a past verb shift the tenses back one step and use statement order for questions.

topics.title: Parts of speech, gerunds, infinitives and confusable words
points: The eight parts of speech are noun, pronoun, verb, adjective, adverb, preposition, conjunction and interjection. Many usage questions reduce to asking which part of speech a blank needs: after an article it needs a noun phrase, and after a linking verb an adjective.

Some verbs take only a gerund (avoid, enjoy, finish, mind, consider, suggest): She avoided answering. Others take only an infinitive (decide, hope, agree, refuse, plan): They decided to leave. A few change meaning: stop smoking (quit) versus stop to smoke (pause in order to smoke).
After a preposition the verb is a gerund, including after the preposition to in look forward to, object to and be used to: I look forward to meeting you, not to meet you.

Word-class pairs that are often confused: affect (verb) and effect (usually a noun); advice (noun) and advise (verb); principal (main, or a head of school) and principle (a rule); complement (to complete) and compliment (praise); lose (verb) and loose (adjective).
Verb-noun agreement extends to determiners and nouns: this kind of error but these kinds of errors; a number of students are, but the number of students is.

lesson.why: Many usage blanks reduce to naming the part of speech the blank needs, or to picking between look-alike words. A short test for each pair settles them.
lesson.intro: Every word has a job in a sentence: a noun names a thing, a verb gives an action or state, an adjective describes a noun, and a preposition links a noun to the rest. Some words sound alike but have different jobs. 'Their' shows ownership, 'there' names a place, and 'they're' is a short way to write 'they are'. Choosing the right one means asking what job the blank has to do.

definitions.meaning: The job a word does in a sentence, such as noun, verb, adjective or preposition.
A shortened form with an apostrophe that replaces letters, such as they're for they are.

principle.text: Replace the blank with a test phrase. If 'they are' fits, write they're; if 'belonging to them' fits, write their; if 'that place' fits, write there. Beside means next to, and besides means in addition to.

lesson.limits: The substitution test works only for these homophones. Other confusable pairs, such as affect and effect or principal and principle, differ in meaning and not just in sound, and the test phrase for those is the meaning itself: affect is a verb, effect is usually a noun.

example.problem: Fill the blanks: ______ sure ______ team has finished ______ work.
steps: Blank 1 must be a subject plus verb: 'they are' fits, so it is They're.
Blank 2 comes before the noun 'team' and shows ownership: their.
Blank 3 is also ownership: 'that place' does not fit, 'belonging to them' does, so it is their again.
example.result: They're sure their team has finished their work.

misconceptions: Using 'there' for ownership because it sounds the same. Ownership before a noun is always 'their'.
Treating 'beside' and 'besides' as spelling variants. 'Beside' means next to; 'besides' means in addition to.

recall.q: What does 'they're' stand for?
recall.a: 'They are'; it must be followed by a word that completes a verb phrase or describes them.

recall.q: How do 'beside' and 'besides' differ?
recall.a: 'Beside' means next to; 'besides' means in addition to or apart from.

recall.q: Which test phrase shows that 'their' is the right word?
recall.a: 'Belonging to them' fits the blank: their team.

practice.stem: Choose the sentence in which every word is correct.
options: Their coming here, besides the lab, because there late.
They're late, so their bus must be over there.
There late, so they're bus must be over their.
Their late, so there bus must be over they're.
practice.explanation: 'They're late' means 'they are late', 'their bus' shows ownership, and 'over there' names a place. The other options tempt because the words sound the same, but each uses at least one spelling in the wrong job, such as 'there bus' or 'over their'.

lesson.summary: Name the job of the blank and use the test phrase: they are, belonging to them, or that place; beside means next to and besides means in addition to.

topics.title: Vocabulary in context and fill in the blanks
points: The aptitude section rarely asks a word's meaning in isolation; it embeds the word in a sentence. The same word shifts meaning with context: fast can mean quick, a period without food, or (of colours) not fading.

Solve a blank in three steps: find the clue phrase (anticipating issues before they occur points to proactive), decide the polarity and degree the blank needs, then plug each option back in to test grammar and collocation.

Denotation is a word's dictionary meaning and connotation its emotional colour: thrifty and stingy both mean careful with money, but thrifty praises and stingy criticises. Pick the option whose connotation matches the sentence's attitude.

Register matters: formal prose takes commence and ascertain where informal speech uses start and find out. An option can be a near synonym and still be wrong because its register or collocation clashes with the sentence.

Words that recur in GATE stems include obfuscate (make unclear), loquacious (talkative), taciturn (reserved, saying little), pragmatic (practical), ambivalent (holding mixed feelings), ephemeral (short-lived) and mitigate (lessen).
In double-blank items, eliminate on the easier blank first, then check that the surviving pair keeps the sentence logically consistent.

lesson.why: Fill-in-the-blank and synonym items reward reading the sentence, not memorising word lists. A blank has a clue in the sentence, and finding it removes most options before any vocabulary is needed.
lesson.intro: A sentence with a blank is a small puzzle. The rest of the sentence tells you what kind of word is missing: whether it should be positive or negative, strong or mild, and which part of speech. First read for that clue, then try each option in the gap. A word can fit the meaning and still be wrong because it does not combine naturally with its neighbours, as 'nearly missed' does and 'utterly missed' in the same slot does not.

definitions.meaning: A word or phrase elsewhere in the sentence that signals the meaning, tone or direction of the missing word.
A pair or group of words that are habitually used together, such as 'revolves around' or 'make a decision'.
The feeling a word carries beyond its dictionary meaning; 'thrifty' praises and 'stingy' criticises.

principle.text: Pick the option that agrees with the clue in meaning and polarity, has the right degree of strength, is the right part of speech, and forms a natural collocation with the words around it. When two options survive, the one that sounds natural beside its neighbours wins.

lesson.limits: Elimination by clue fails when the sentence offers no clue, as in a bare synonym question such as 'a word similar to hasten'. There, rely on the meaning you know, and check each option against the given words instead of the sentence.

example.problem: Choose the word that fills the blank: 'Although the first draft was careless, the final report was remarkably ______.'
steps: Find the signal: 'Although' sets two ideas against each other, so the blank must contrast with 'careless'.
State the needed meaning: careful, accurate, thorough. It is positive and describes a document.
Test options such as 'meticulous', 'sloppy', 'hasty' and 'vague'. The last three keep the negative tone and are removed; 'meticulous' fits.
example.result: 'Meticulous' is the answer, chosen because the contrast word reverses the polarity.

misconceptions: Choosing the first word whose meaning looks close, without testing it in the sentence. A near synonym can clash in degree, tone or collocation.
Treating homophones such as fare and fair as interchangeable. Spelling and part of speech are part of the answer, so read the sentence before settling on a spelling.
Ignoring the grammar of the blank. If the gap needs an adverb, an adjective option is wrong however good its meaning.

recall.q: What are the first two things to read in a fill-in-the-blank sentence?
recall.a: The clue phrase that signals meaning and the polarity (positive or negative) the blank needs.

recall.q: What is a collocation?
recall.a: Words that are habitually used together, so that a close synonym of one of them can still sound wrong.

recall.q: Why do 'thrifty' and 'stingy' differ although both describe careful spending?
recall.a: They share a denotation but differ in connotation: thrifty approves, stingy disapproves.

practice.stem: Choose the best word: 'The committee's decision was so ______ that nobody could tell what it actually required.'
practice.explanation: The clause 'nobody could tell what it required' is the clue: the decision was unclear, and 'ambiguous' means open to more than one reading. 'Decisive' tempts because the sentence is about a decision, but a decisive decision would be easy to understand. 'Generous' and 'punctual' have nothing to do with clarity.

lesson.summary: Read the clue and the polarity first, then check meaning, degree, part of speech and collocation for each option; near synonyms are eliminated by tone and fit.

topics.title: Idioms, phrases and one-word substitutes
points: An idiom means something other than its literal words. Common ones: at the drop of a hat (immediately, without hesitation), bite the bullet (face something painful but necessary), burn the midnight oil (work late into the night) and cut corners (do something cheaply or carelessly).

More idioms that recur: beat around the bush (avoid the main point), break the ice (ease initial tension), a blessing in disguise (a misfortune that turns out well), the last straw (the final problem that makes a situation unbearable), down in the dumps (unhappy), hit the nail on the head (state exactly what is right).
Idiom questions usually ask which sentence uses the idiom correctly, so check that the surrounding situation matches the idiom's meaning and tone.

One-word substitutes compress a definition into one word: omnivore (eats both plants and animals), narcissist (excessively admires oneself), philatelist (collects stamps), misanthrope (dislikes humankind), polyglot (speaks many languages), insolvent (unable to pay debts), anonymous (of unknown name).

lesson.why: Idiom and phrase items test whether you know a fixed expression's real meaning. Reading the words literally leads to the wrong choice every time, so a short list of common idioms pays off.
lesson.intro: An idiom is a fixed group of words whose meaning cannot be worked out from the separate words. 'Bite the bullet' has nothing to do with bullets; it means to face something unpleasant that cannot be avoided. A one-word substitute is the opposite move: a single word that stands for a whole description, such as 'polyglot' for a person who speaks many languages. In both, you must recall the meaning, then check that it fits the situation in the sentence.

definitions.meaning: A fixed expression whose overall meaning differs from the literal meaning of its words.
A single word that replaces a longer phrase or definition.

'Keep one's head down' means stay out of trouble, 'have a head for' something means have a natural ability for it, and 'a cool head on one's shoulders' means calm good judgement. The small words down, for and on are fixed.

principle.text: To answer an idiom or phrase item, find the figurative meaning of the expression, then test that meaning against the situation and tone of each sentence or blank. Part of an idiom cannot be changed: the prepositions and small words are fixed, as in 'keep one's head down' (stay out of trouble), 'a head for' (a natural talent for) and 'a cool head on one's shoulders' (calm good sense).

lesson.limits: An idiom is not always figurative. 'Keep your head down' can be literal advice to stoop, so when the sentence describes a physical action, take the literal reading. Also, many idioms have a small set of correct forms, so a plausible preposition is not enough.

example.problem: Which sentence uses 'a blessing in disguise' correctly? (a) The rain was a blessing in disguise, because it stopped the match we were sure to lose and gave us time to practise. (b) He wore a blessing in disguise at the party.
steps: Recall the meaning: a misfortune that later turns out to be good.
Check (a): rain is an apparent misfortune, and the result, time to practise, is good. The meaning fits.
Check (b): the phrase is used as a physical object, which no meaning of the idiom allows.

misconceptions: Explaining an idiom from its separate words. The meaning belongs to the whole expression.
Accepting any preposition that sounds right. In an idiom the small words are fixed, and a different one makes the phrase wrong.
Confusing a one-word substitute with a near relative. A 'misanthrope' dislikes people in general, which is different from someone who is merely shy.

recall.q: What does 'bite the bullet' mean?
recall.a: To face something painful or unpleasant that cannot be avoided.

recall.q: What is a one-word substitute?
recall.a: A single word that stands for a longer description, such as polyglot for a person who speaks many languages.

recall.q: Why can you not replace a preposition inside an idiom?
recall.a: The idiom is fixed as a whole, so changing a small word breaks the phrase.

practice.stem: Which sentence uses 'beat around the bush' correctly?
options: The gardener beat around the bush to remove the weeds.
Stop beating around the bush and tell me whether you got the job.
She beat around the bush with great speed.
He beat around the bush and won the race.
practice.explanation: 'Beat around the bush' means to avoid the main point, and the second sentence asks someone to stop avoiding it. The first option tempts because it reads the idiom literally, which suits a garden. The last two use the phrase where the meaning of avoiding a topic makes no sense.

lesson.summary: Learn an idiom or substitute by its meaning as a whole, then check that the meaning matches the situation and that the fixed small words are unchanged.

topics.title: Word roots and word analogies
points: Latin and Greek roots let you estimate an unfamiliar word: mal- means bad (malign, malicious, malfunction, maladroit), bene- means good (benevolent, benefactor, benign), dict- means speak (dictate, contradict, predict).
Roots mislead when a word only looks like it contains them: malleable comes from a root meaning hammer and means easily shaped, not bad. Confirm a root guess against the sentence before trusting it.

An analogy A : B :: C : D holds when D relates to C exactly as B relates to A. State the A–B relation as a sentence first, such as an archipelago is a group of islands, then test each option in the same sentence.
Common analogy relations: part to whole, member to group, worker to tool, cause to effect, degree (warm : hot), synonym and antonym. Distractors often share a topic with C but not the relation.

lesson.why: Roots let you guess the meaning of an unfamiliar word, and analogies test whether you can name the relation between two words and apply it again. Both reward stating a relation in a plain sentence.
lesson.intro: Many English words are built from roots taken from Latin and Greek. If you know that 'mal-' means bad and 'dict-' means speak, you can guess something about 'malicious' and 'predict'. A word analogy such as 'A : B :: C : D' says that D relates to C in the same way B relates to A. The method is to put the first pair into a sentence, for example 'a fast is a stronger form of a diet', and then find the option that fits the same sentence.

definitions.meaning: The core part of a word that carries its basic meaning, often borrowed from Latin or Greek.
A pair-of-pairs comparison in which the second pair has the same relation as the first.
A series of words ordered from weaker to stronger, such as dry, arid, parched.

principle.text: For an analogy, name the relation in the first pair (synonym, antonym, degree, part to whole, worker to tool, cause to effect), then pick the option that completes the second pair with the same relation in the same direction. For a root, use it to form a guess and confirm the guess in the sentence.

lesson.limits: Roots mislead when a word only looks like it holds the root: 'malleable' comes from a word for hammer and means easily shaped, not bad. An analogy also fails if the direction is reversed, so 'walk, jog, sprint' rising in speed needs a rising third term.

example.problem: If the arrow means 'increasing in intensity', complete the chain: warm → hot → scorching is analogous to pleased → delighted → ______. Options: ecstatic, annoyed, content, neutral.
steps: State the relation in the first chain: each word is a stronger degree of the same condition, here heat.
Apply it to pleased → delighted: both are positive, and delighted is stronger. The next word must be stronger still.
Test the options. 'Annoyed' is negative, and 'content' and 'neutral' are weaker than delighted. Only 'ecstatic' continues upward.

misconceptions: Choosing the option from the same topic as the third word without checking the relation. A distractor often shares a theme but not the relation.
Applying a root rule blindly. A word that contains 'mal' is not necessarily negative.
Ignoring direction. In an intensity chain, an option that is milder than the previous word breaks the pattern.

recall.q: How do you start every analogy question?
recall.a: Put the relation in the first pair into a sentence, then test each option against that sentence.

recall.q: What do the roots mal- and bene- mean?
recall.a: Mal- means bad and bene- means good.

recall.q: Give a word where a root guess misleads.
recall.a: Malleable: it looks like it contains mal-, but it means easily shaped.

practice.stem: Complete the analogy: bright : brilliant :: tired : ______
practice.explanation: Brilliant is a stronger degree of bright, so the blank must be a stronger degree of tired, and 'exhausted' is. 'Sleepy' tempts because it belongs to the same topic, but it is no stronger than tired. 'Energetic' and 'awake' are opposites and break the relation.

lesson.summary: Name the relation and its direction in the first pair before reading the options; use roots only as a guess to confirm in the sentence.

topics.title: Reading comprehension: method and question types
points: Skim first: read the first and last sentence of each paragraph to find the theme. Then read the question, take its keywords and scan the passage for them. Answer from the lines around the keyword, not from memory of the passage.

Question types are main idea, author's tone, inference, vocabulary in context and logical completion. A main-idea answer covers the whole passage; an option that covers only one example is too narrow, and one that covers the whole field is too broad.

Tone comes from loaded words: disastrous, tragic, brilliant and flawless signal strong emotion, while measured, observed and recorded signal neutrality. Deciding whether the author criticises, praises or reports usually eliminates half the options.
For vocabulary in context, replace the word with each option and keep the one that preserves the sentence's meaning in that passage, even when a different option is the more common dictionary sense.

lesson.why: Reading comprehension questions reward a fixed routine more than speed reading: the same few question types recur, and each has a standard way to find or eliminate the answer.
lesson.intro: A comprehension passage is a short text followed by questions that must be answered only from that text. Reading every word slowly wastes time, so the routine is to get the theme first and then return to the lines a question points to. The questions themselves fall into a few kinds: what the passage is mostly about, how the author feels, what follows from it, what a word means in context, and how a sentence should be completed.

definitions.meaning: Reading quickly, usually the first and last sentence of each paragraph, to find the theme.
Looking through the passage for a keyword taken from the question.
The author's attitude, shown by loaded words such as disastrous or brilliant versus neutral ones such as observed.

principle.text: Skim for the theme, read the question, take its keywords and scan the passage, then answer from the lines around the keyword. A main-idea option must cover the whole passage: one that covers only an example is too narrow, and one that covers the whole field is too broad.

lesson.limits: Skimming finds the theme but not details, so a detail or inference question still needs the lines around its keyword. For vocabulary in context, the common dictionary meaning can be wrong; the meaning that keeps the sentence intact in this passage wins.

example.problem: A passage says: "The committee's report, though thorough, was ignored by those who needed it most." A question asks the author's tone. Options: (a) celebratory  (b) mildly critical  (c) neutral  (d) hostile.
steps: Look for loaded words: "thorough" praises the report, while "ignored by those who needed it most" regrets how it was treated.
The criticism is aimed at the readers, but it is gentle, with no strong emotional words.
Eliminate (a) because nothing is celebrated, (c) because the regret is clear, and (d) because the wording is not hostile.
example.result: The tone is mildly critical, option (b).

misconceptions: Answering from memory of the passage. The answer must come from the lines around the question's keyword, since memory blends in your own ideas.
Choosing the most dramatic option for a tone question. Strong words in the options often do not match a measured passage.

recall.q: What is the order of the reading method?
recall.a: Skim for the theme, read the question, pick its keywords, scan the passage for them and answer from the surrounding lines.

recall.q: Why is a main-idea option rejected for being too narrow?
recall.a: It covers only one example or detail rather than the whole passage.

recall.q: How is a vocabulary-in-context question solved?
recall.a: Substitute each option for the word and keep the one that preserves the sentence's meaning in that passage.

practice.stem: A passage describes how three different cities cut traffic using congestion charges, and ends by recommending the approach. Which is the best statement of its main idea?
options: Congestion charges worked in one city.
All urban problems can be solved by pricing.
Congestion charges have helped cities reduce traffic and are worth adopting.
Traffic is a growing problem worldwide.
practice.explanation: The passage covers three cities and ends with a recommendation, so the main idea combines the result and the recommendation. The first option is too narrow because it covers a single city. The second tempts as a bold summary but is too broad, since the passage says nothing about all urban problems.

lesson.summary: Skim for the theme, scan from the question's keywords, answer from nearby lines, and test main-idea options against the whole passage so that neither the narrow nor the over-broad choice is taken.

topics.title: Inference questions and their traps
points: An inference must follow strictly from the text with no outside assumption. If an option needs a fact the passage never states, eliminate it however true it is in the real world.

Extreme options with always, never, all, none or must usually overstate a nuanced passage. They are correct only when the passage itself is absolute, so compare the strength of the option with the strength of the text.
Out-of-scope options bring in a new topic, time frame or group, such as claiming that battery technology is advancing when the passage only says storage is costly now.

An implication does not run backwards: from Every library opened after the policy offers evening hours you cannot infer that every library with evening hours opened after the policy. The valid form is the contrapositive.
Some X are Y guarantees at least one X exists, but it says nothing about whether all X are Y or about X that are not Y.

lesson.why: Reading and inference questions are decided by what the passage actually supports. Most wrong options are true-sounding statements that go beyond the text, so knowing the standard traps wins marks.
lesson.intro: An inference question asks what must be true given the passage. You are not asked what is true in the world or what the author might like. The right option follows from the sentences you were given, using nothing else. Wrong options usually fall into a few shapes: they claim more than the passage says, bring in a new topic, or reverse a one-way statement. Learning those shapes lets you reject options quickly.

definitions.meaning: A conclusion that follows from the text alone, with no outside fact or assumption.
An option using words such as always, never, all or none, which is stronger than the text supports.
An option about a topic, group or time that the passage does not discuss.
The reversal of an if-then statement. It does not follow from the original.

principle.text: Accept an option only if the passage forces it. Reject options that need an outside fact, state a stronger claim than the text, change the topic or time frame, or reverse an implication. From 'if P then Q' you may conclude 'if not Q then not P', but not 'if Q then P'.

lesson.limits: A strong word is acceptable when the passage itself is strong: if the text says 'no applicant was accepted', then 'none' is correct. Treat the extreme-option rule as a warning to compare strengths, not as a ban on absolutes.

example.problem: Passage: 'Every course that uses the new software finishes its syllabus early.' Which follows: (a) Every course that finishes early uses the new software. (b) A course that did not finish early does not use the new software.
steps: Write the passage as an implication: uses software, so finishes early.
Option (a) is the converse: finishes early, so uses software. An implication does not run backwards, since other courses may finish early for other reasons.
Option (b) is the contrapositive: not finishing early, so not using the software. It is logically equivalent to the passage.

misconceptions: Choosing an option because it is true in real life. The passage must support it.
Treating 'some' as 'all'. 'Some X are Y' guarantees at least one case, and says nothing about the rest.
Rejecting every option with a strong word. It is correct when the passage uses a matching strong word.

Picking the option that sounds closest in wording. Match an option to a paraphrase of the passage, and strike it if one word contradicts the text. Hedge words such as 'seemingly' or 'supposedly' show the author doubts the claim.

recall.q: What is a strict inference?
recall.a: A conclusion that follows from the passage alone, using no outside fact.

recall.q: Why is the converse of an implication unsafe?
recall.a: From 'if P then Q' you cannot conclude 'if Q then P', because Q may have other causes.

recall.q: Name two shapes of wrong option.
recall.a: An extreme option that overstates the passage, and an out-of-scope option that brings in a new topic.

recall.q: What does a hedge word such as 'seemingly' tell you about the author?
recall.a: That the author doubts or distances themselves from the claim, so the stance is not plain agreement.

practice.stem: Passage: 'Only members who paid by March can vote.' Which statement must be true?
options: Every member who paid by March votes.
A person who did not pay by March cannot vote.
Anyone who can vote is a member who paid late.
Nobody who paid by March can be refused a vote.
practice.explanation: The passage says paying by March is needed for voting, so someone who did not pay cannot vote. The first option tempts because it reverses the statement into a guarantee, but paying only makes voting possible, not certain. The third contradicts the passage and the fourth claims a stronger guarantee than the text gives.

lesson.summary: A valid inference is forced by the text. Reject outside facts, overstated claims, new topics and reversed implications; keep the contrapositive.

topics.title: Contrast and transition signals
points: Contrast words (however, although, though, despite, in spite of, nevertheless, yet, conversely, whereas) reverse the direction of the logic. The key information in a passage, and the answer to most inference questions, usually sits right after them.

Cause and result words (therefore, thus, hence, consequently, as a result) continue the logic: the blank after them must follow from what came before. Addition words (furthermore, moreover, in addition, also) add a point in the same direction.

Grammar of the signals: despite and in spite of take a noun or gerund (despite the rain, despite being tired), while although takes a full clause (although it rained). However and nevertheless after a semicolon take a comma: She was exhausted; nevertheless, she kept running.

Polarity test for a blank: if the clause before the contrast word is positive, the blank after it is negative, and the reverse. For example, Despite the manager's ___ approach, the team delivered on time needs a negative word such as tyrannical.

lesson.why: Words such as however, although and therefore tell you which way the argument turns. Reading them first lets you predict the polarity of a blank and solves many fill-in items without difficult vocabulary.
lesson.intro: A transition word is a small connecting word that shows how two ideas relate. Some reverse the direction ('however', 'although', 'but'), some continue it ('therefore', 'so', 'also'). In a sentence with a blank, the signal tells you whether the missing word should agree with the first part or oppose it. For example, 'but' after a positive statement means the blank is negative. That prediction narrows the options before you read them.

definitions.meaning: A word that reverses direction between two ideas, such as but, however, although, yet or whereas.
A word that shows a result follows from what came before, such as therefore, thus, hence or consequently.
Whether a word or clause is positive or negative in tone.

principle.text: After a contrast word, the next idea has the opposite polarity to the one before. After a causal or addition word, it has the same polarity. Predict the polarity of the blank from the signal, then choose the option that matches. The opposite can be one of meaning as well as of sign: after 'but', the blank may need the reverse of a named word, such as an unplanned approach set against an organised one.

lesson.limits: The rule needs a clear polarity to start with. If the first clause is neutral, such as 'The report was long, but ______', a contrast word does not fix the answer, so use other clues. Grammar also matters: 'despite' takes a noun or an -ing form, while 'although' takes a full clause. When the contrast is between two named qualities, the target word is not necessarily negative, so find the word it opposes and pick the option that means the reverse.

example.problem: Choose the word: 'The plan looked flawless on paper; nevertheless, in practice it proved ______.' Options: workable, unrealistic, brilliant, effortless.
steps: Find the signal: 'nevertheless' reverses direction.
The first clause is positive (flawless), so the blank must be negative.
Remove 'workable', 'brilliant' and 'effortless', which are positive. 'Unrealistic' is negative and fits.

misconceptions: Reading a contrast word as a continuation. 'But' and 'though' always turn the sentence.
Mixing the grammar of 'although' and 'despite'. 'Despite' needs a noun or -ing form, so 'despite it rained' is wrong.
Choosing a word because it sounds strong, instead of because it has the polarity the signal demands.

recall.q: What does a contrast word do to polarity?
recall.a: It reverses it: a positive first clause is followed by a negative idea, and the reverse.

recall.q: Name three causal connectors.
recall.a: Therefore, thus and hence (also consequently).

recall.q: How do 'although' and 'despite' differ in grammar?
recall.a: Although takes a full clause; despite takes a noun or an -ing form.

recall.q: What if the blank is not clearly positive or negative after a contrast word?
recall.a: Find the named word it contrasts with and choose the option that means the opposite of that word.

practice.stem: Choose the word: 'She is a gifted speaker, yet her written work is surprisingly ______.'
practice.explanation: 'Yet' reverses the direction after the positive clause 'gifted speaker', so the blank must be negative, and 'weak' is the only negative option. 'Polished' and 'elegant' tempt because they match the praise earlier in the sentence, which is the polarity the signal rules out.

lesson.summary: Contrast words flip polarity and causal or addition words keep it; predict the sign of the blank from the signal before you look at the options.

topics.title: Narrative sequencing and paragraph coherence
points: A coherent paragraph has a topic sentence that introduces the subject, supporting sentences that develop it, and a conclusion that closes it. Jumbled-sentence questions ask you to rebuild that order.

The opener names its subject in full and depends on nothing earlier. A sentence that starts with a pronoun (it, they, this), a definite reference (the device, such a plan) or a connector (however, as a result) cannot come first.

Build pairs, not whole orders: link each pronoun to the noun it replaces and each connector to the idea it answers. However needs a claim to oppose; as a result needs a cause. Two or three fixed pairs usually leave one option.
Use the options: once the opener is known, discard options that start differently, then test the remaining orders only at the pairs where they differ.
Chronology and general-to-specific movement settle the remaining ties: an event comes before its consequence, and a broad claim before its example.

lesson.why: Sequencing items ask you to rebuild a paragraph from jumbled sentences. Marks come from spotting links between sentences rather than reading for general meaning.
lesson.intro: A paragraph has an order: it opens by introducing a subject, develops it, and ends with a conclusion. In a jumbled set, each sentence still carries hints about where it belongs. A pronoun such as 'it' needs an earlier noun. A connector such as 'however' needs an earlier claim. A sentence that names its subject in full and depends on nothing is a likely opener. Find these hints, join sentences into pairs, and then use the answer options to settle the order.

definitions.meaning: The first sentence, which names its subject in full and relies on no earlier sentence.
Two sentences that must sit together because the second refers back to the first through a pronoun, a connector or a repeated idea.
The quality of a paragraph in which each sentence follows from the one before.

principle.text: Pick the opener first: it cannot begin with a pronoun, a definite reference to something unnamed, or a connector. Then build pairs from pronouns and connectors, keep events in time order and general claims before examples, and discard options that break a pair.

lesson.limits: Several sentences can look like openers, and some paragraphs have no connectors at all. Then rely on time order and on the broad-to-specific order, and use the options to compare only the places where they differ.

example.problem: Order these: P: Without that seed, the harvest failed. Q: The monsoon arrived a month late this year. R: Farmers who had sown early lost their seed to it. S: The shortfall pushed prices in the market up sharply.
steps: Find the opener: Q names its subject in full. R needs 'it' to have an antecedent, P needs 'that seed' to have one, and S needs a 'shortfall'.
Link cause and effect: the late monsoon (Q) is what 'it' means in R, and the seed lost in R is the 'that seed' of P. Q P R fails because P would mention seed before R introduces it.
Place S last: the 'shortfall' is the failed harvest in P, and rising prices are its consequence.
example.result: The order is Q R P S.

misconceptions: Starting with the sentence that sounds most general, even though it begins with 'this' or 'however'.
Ordering by topic alone. Pronouns, connectors and time order decide the sequence.
Testing every option in full instead of checking the fixed pairs, which usually leaves one option.

recall.q: Which kinds of sentence cannot be the opener?
recall.a: A sentence starting with a pronoun, a definite reference to something unnamed, or a connector such as however.

recall.q: What is a mandatory pair?
recall.a: Two sentences that must be adjacent because the second refers back to the first by a pronoun or connector.

recall.q: Which two orderings settle remaining ties?
recall.a: Chronology (events before consequences) and general before specific.

practice.stem: Order the sentences. P: He then replaced it with a new one himself. Q: Arun bought an old house at the edge of the town, hoping to move in at once. R: Its roof, however, had caved in during the last monsoon. S: Soon the house was ready to live in.
practice.explanation: Q opens because it names Arun and the house in full and states his hope. R follows with 'however', which opposes that hope of moving in at once. P's 'it' can only mean the caved-in roof from R, so P comes after R, and S ends with the result, so QRPS holds. QPRS tempts because P and R are both about the roof, but 'it' in P has no antecedent in Q.

lesson.summary: Find the opener, join sentences through pronouns and connectors, keep time and broad-to-specific order, and use the options to settle what is left.

formulas.name: Zero and first conditional
formulas.text: If + present, present (general truth); If + present, will + V1 (real future)
where: base or present form of the verb
formulas.note: Never put will in the if-clause for a future condition: If it rains tomorrow, not If it will rain tomorrow.

formulas.name: Second conditional (unreal present)
formulas.note: With be, formal usage takes were for every person: If I were you, I would accept.

formulas.name: Third conditional (unreal past)
formulas.text: If + had + V3, would have + V3
formulas.note: The trap is If I would have studied: would have belongs only in the result clause.

formulas.name: Proximity rule for either…or / neither…nor
formulas.tex: \text{neither } S_1 \text{ nor } S_2 + \text{verb agreeing with } S_2
formulas.text: neither S1 nor S2 + verb agreeing with S2 (the nearer subject)
where: the two subjects joined by the correlative
formulas.note: Contrast with both…and, which always takes a plural verb, and with as well as or along with, where the verb agrees with the first subject.

formulas.name: Tense backshift in reported speech
formulas.text: present → past, past and present perfect → past perfect, will → would, can → could
formulas.note: Applies after a past reporting verb (said, asked). A universal truth may keep its tense: He said that water boils at 100 °C.

formulas.name: Analogy test
formulas.tex: A : B :: C : D \iff R(A, B) = R(C, D)
formulas.text: A : B :: C : D holds exactly when the relation R from A to B is the relation from C to D
where: the relation stated as a sentence, such as A is a group of B
formulas.note: Write R as a full sentence before reading the options; a distractor usually matches C's topic but not R.

formulas.name: Order of stacked adjectives
formulas.text: opinion → size → age → shape → colour → origin → material → purpose → noun
where: a noun-like modifier naming the use, as in dining table or running shoes
formulas.note: Adjectives from the same class (two opinions) are separated by a comma or and; adjectives from different classes take no comma: a beautiful old Italian wooden table.

problemTypes.title: Choose the word that best fills the blank
recipe: Find the clue phrase or signal word (despite, because, so…that, a definition after a comma).
Decide what the blank needs: polarity (positive or negative), degree (mild or strong) and part of speech.
Eliminate options with the wrong polarity, then plug the survivors in and keep the one that fits grammar and collocation.
problemTypes.trap: A literal synonym of the clue word can still be wrong if it does not fit the sentence grammatically or carries the wrong connotation.

problemTypes.title: Grammatically correct sentence or correct verb form
recipe: Strip prepositional phrases and relative clauses to expose the true subject and verb.
Check agreement, then tense against the time markers, then articles, prepositions and modifiers.
For either/neither…or/nor match the nearer subject; for each/every/one of use the singular.
problemTypes.trap: A plural noun inside of … sits right before the verb and pulls the eye toward a plural verb.

problemTypes.title: Fill the blank with the right article, preposition, pronoun or verb form
recipe: Read the words on both sides of the blank and decide which part of speech it needs: a noun phrase after an article, an adjective after a linking verb, a gerund after a preposition.
Apply the matching rule: a or an by first sound, in/on/at by size of the time or place, pronoun case by deleting the other noun, gerund or infinitive by the governing verb.
Check the tense against every time marker in the sentence, then re-read the whole sentence with the chosen option.
problemTypes.trap: Reading to in look forward to, object to or be used to as an infinitive marker, which gives look forward to meet instead of look forward to meeting.

problemTypes.title: Idiom meaning, correct idiom usage or word analogy
recipe: For an idiom, recall its figurative meaning and check that the situation in each option matches it in meaning and tone.
For an analogy, state the first pair's relation as a sentence and apply the same sentence to each option.
problemTypes.trap: Options on the topic of the second pair but with a different relation: in Archipelago : Islands :: Constellation : ?, Sky is where a constellation is seen (location), not what it is made of (members).

problemTypes.title: Which statement can be inferred from the passage
recipe: Read the question first, then the passage, marking contrast words and quantifiers (all, some, only).
Eliminate options with extreme wording the text does not support and options that need outside facts.
Among the survivors, keep the one that restates a limited claim of the passage; check it is not the converse of a stated rule.
problemTypes.trap: The converse of a passage rule, or a real-world truth the passage never asserts, looks like an inference but does not follow.

problemTypes.title: Author's tone or main idea of a passage
recipe: Collect the loaded adjectives and adverbs; they reveal whether the author criticises, praises or reports.
For main idea, reject options that cover only one example (too narrow) or the whole field (too broad).
problemTypes.trap: A praise word attached to one group (the team's effort) does not make the author's view of the main subject positive.

problemTypes.title: Arrange the jumbled sentences into a coherent paragraph
recipe: Find the opener: the sentence that introduces the subject without a pronoun, a definite back-reference or a connector.
Fix mandatory pairs: pronoun after its noun, however after the claim it opposes, as a result after its cause.
Discard options that break any fixed pair; the one left is the answer.
problemTypes.trap: A sentence that opens with a connector such as however or as a result can never be first.

questions.stem: Choose the option that correctly fills the blank: Neither the manager nor the employees ______ aware of the upcoming changes.
questions.explanation: With neither…nor the verb agrees with the nearer subject. The subject next to the verb is employees, which is plural, so the verb is are. Is, was and has been are all singular forms and would fit only if the order were reversed (Neither the employees nor the manager is aware).

questions.stem: Select all the sentences that are grammatically correct.
options: Each of the students has submitted the form.
Every one of the servers are running.
Neither of the proposals was accepted.
The committee has published its report.
questions.explanation: Each of, every one of and neither of (used alone) take singular verbs, because the real subject is each, every one or neither, not the plural noun after of. So has submitted and was accepted are right, and are running must be is running. The committee acts as one body here, so the singular has published with its is correct.

questions.stem: Choose the word that best fills the blank: Despite the manager's ______ approach, the team delivered the project on time.
questions.explanation: Despite signals that the two halves contrast. Delivering on time is a positive outcome, so the blank must be negative. Supportive, benevolent and optimistic are all positive, so a positive outcome would be expected with them and despite would make no sense. Tyrannical is the only negative option.

questions.stem: Choose the word that best fills the blank: He is known for his ______ approach to problem-solving, always anticipating issues before they occur.
questions.explanation: The clue phrase anticipating issues before they occur describes forward-looking, preventive action, which is the meaning of proactive. Retroactive means applying to the past, the opposite direction. Destructive and superficial do not match anticipating anything.

questions.stem: Choose the option that correctly fills the blank: If she ______ the earlier train, she would have reached the hall before the speech began.
questions.explanation: The result clause would have reached describes an unreal past, which is the third conditional: if + past perfect, would have + V3. The if-clause therefore needs had caught. Caught gives the second-conditional if-clause, which pairs with would reach. Would catch never belongs in an if-clause, and has caught is a present perfect that does not describe an unreal past.
