questions.stem: Choose the option that fills the three blanks correctly: ______ honest official and ______ European delegate attended ______ meeting that the ministry had announced.
questions.explanation: Articles follow the first sound, not the first letter. Honest begins with a silent h and a vowel sound, so it takes an. European begins with a y sound (a consonant sound), so it takes a. The meeting is a specific one, defined by the clause that the ministry had announced, so it takes the.

questions.stem: Choose the option that correctly completes the sentence: Walking to the station, ______
options: the rain began to fall heavily.
my umbrella was left at home.
I realised that I had left my umbrella at home.
it started to rain on me.
questions.explanation: The opening phrase Walking to the station has no subject of its own, so the subject of the main clause must be whoever was walking. Only I can walk. The rain, my umbrella and it cannot walk, so options A, B and D leave the modifier dangling.

questions.stem: Select all the words that can correctly fill the blank: She was entirely exhausted; ______, she kept running toward the finish line.
questions.explanation: Exhaustion would normally make someone stop, so continuing to run is a contrast. Nevertheless and however both signal contrast and fit after a semicolon with a comma. Therefore and consequently signal a result, which would claim that she kept running because she was exhausted.

questions.stem: Select all the sentences in which the idiom is used correctly.
options: He agrees to help at the drop of a hat, so we always ask him first.
She burnt the midnight oil and finished the report just before dawn.
We bit the bullet and accepted the painful but necessary budget cuts.
After winning the scholarship, he was down in the dumps all week.
questions.explanation: At the drop of a hat means immediately and without hesitation, which fits someone always ready to help. Burning the midnight oil means working late into the night, which fits finishing before dawn. Biting the bullet means accepting something painful but necessary, which fits budget cuts. Down in the dumps means unhappy, which contradicts winning a scholarship, so option D misuses it.

questions.stem: Read the statement: "While solar energy is abundant, current battery storage technology makes it financially unviable for small rural homes." Which of the following can be inferred from the statement?
options: Rural homes will never use solar energy.
Storage costs are a barrier for a specific group of users.
questions.explanation: The statement limits its claim to small rural homes and to current storage technology. Option A generalises to everywhere and option B uses never, so both overstate a qualified claim. Option D brings in a fact about progress that the statement never mentions. Option C restates the claim without going beyond it: cost, through storage, is a barrier for one group.

questions.stem: "The project was an unmitigated disaster, though the team was praised for its effort." What is the author's attitude toward the project itself?
questions.explanation: Unmitigated disaster is strongly negative language aimed at the project. The praise belongs to the team's effort, a different subject, introduced by though. The attitude toward the project is critical. Admiring confuses the team with the project, and indifferent ignores the loaded phrase.

questions.stem: Arrange the sentences into a coherent paragraph. P: As a result, the town council voted to convert the station into a museum. Q: The old railway station had stood empty for nearly two decades. R: However, a group of residents argued that the building's architecture was worth preserving. S: Developers proposed demolishing it to build a shopping complex.
questions.explanation: Q is the opener: it names the station in full and depends on nothing earlier. S uses it for the station, so it follows Q. R begins with However and opposes the demolition proposal, so it follows S. P begins with As a result and gives the outcome of the residents' argument, so it follows R. The only order meeting all three pairs is QSRP. SQRP opens with a pronoun, QRSP puts However before the proposal it opposes, and QSPR makes the museum a result of the demolition plan.

questions.stem: Archipelago : Islands :: Constellation : ?
questions.explanation: The relation is group to members: an archipelago is a group of islands. A constellation is a group of stars. A galaxy is a larger structure that contains constellations, not their members. Planets are not what constellations are made of, and sky is the background, not the members.

questions.stem: How many of the following words contain the root mal- in the sense of bad? malign, benign, malfunction, malleable, maladroit, benefactor
questions.explanation: Malign (speak badly of), malfunction (work badly) and maladroit (clumsy, badly skilled) use mal- meaning bad. Benign and benefactor use bene- meaning good. Malleable comes from a root meaning hammer and means easily shaped, so it only looks like a mal- word. The count is 3.

questions.stem: How many of the following sentences are grammatically incorrect? (i) She has been working here since Monday. (ii) He is senior than me in the department. (iii) Fewer people attended the workshop this year. (iv) I am knowing the answer to this question. (v) She avoided to answer the reporter's question. (vi) One of my friends live in Pune.
questions.explanation: (i) is correct: since Monday marks a starting point up to now, which needs the present perfect continuous. (ii) is wrong: senior takes to, not than. (iii) is correct: people is countable, so fewer is right. (iv) is wrong: know is a stative verb and takes no continuous form, so I know the answer. (v) is wrong: avoid takes a gerund, so avoided answering. (vi) is wrong: the subject is one, so lives. Four sentences, (ii), (iv), (v) and (vi), are incorrect.

questions.stem: Passage: "Every library in the town that opened after the new policy offers evening hours. Some libraries that offer evening hours also lend laptops. The Central Library opened before the policy." How many of the following statements must be true? (1) Every library that offers evening hours opened after the policy. (2) Any library that opened after the policy offers evening hours. (3) The Central Library does not offer evening hours. (4) At least one library offers evening hours. (5) Some library that lends laptops opened after the policy.
questions.explanation: (1) is the converse of the first sentence and does not follow: a library opened before the policy may still offer evening hours. (2) restates the first sentence, so it must be true. (3) does not follow: the rule says nothing about libraries opened before the policy, so the Central Library may or may not offer evening hours. (4) must be true, because some libraries that offer evening hours exist. (5) does not follow: the laptop-lending libraries could all have opened before the policy. Checking every assignment of the three properties to four libraries that satisfies the passage confirms that only (2) and (4) hold in all of them, so the answer is 2.

questions.stem: Choose the option that correctly completes the sentence: By the time the inspection team arrives next Monday, the faulty pipes ______.
questions.explanation: The replacing finishes before a future point (next Monday), so the tense is the future perfect. Pipes do not replace anything; they are replaced, so the voice is passive: will have been + V3. Will have replaced is active and makes the pipes the doers. Have been replaced is present perfect and clashes with next Monday. Will be replacing is active and continuous, so it is wrong on both counts. Note also that arrives, not will arrive, is right in the by-the-time clause.

questions.stem: Select all the sentences that are grammatically correct.
options: The manager asked Priya and me to review the code.
Between you and I, the plan will fail.
She is one of the engineers who have cleared the test.
Whom do you think is responsible for the outage?
questions.explanation: Delete the other noun to test case: asked me, so Priya and me is right. Between is a preposition and takes the object form: between you and me. In one of the engineers who have cleared, who refers to engineers, which is plural, so have is right. In the last sentence do you think is a parenthetical; the pronoun is the subject of is responsible (he is responsible), so it must be who.

questions.stem: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.
options: No sooner had the results been announced when the website crashed.
Hardly had the meeting begun when the power failed.
Not only she writes the code but also tests it.
Although the server was slow, but the demo succeeded.
questions.explanation: Hardly pairs with when and, placed first, inverts the verb (had the meeting begun), so the second sentence is right. No sooner pairs with than, not when. Not only placed first needs inversion (Not only does she write), or it must move inside: She not only writes the code but also tests it. Although and but are two contrast markers for one contrast; drop one.

questions.stem: Choose the option that fills the blank correctly: She bought a ______ table for the hall.
questions.explanation: Stacked adjectives go opinion, size, age, shape, colour, origin, material, purpose. Beautiful is opinion, old is age, Italian is origin and wooden is material, so the order is beautiful old Italian wooden. Every other option breaks the sequence, for example by placing the material word wooden first.

questions.stem: Each blank takes exactly one of in, on or at. How many blanks take in? The workshop starts ___ Monday ___ 10 a.m. ___ June; the venue is ___ the third floor, and the slides are ___ the shared folder.
questions.explanation: On for days (on Monday), at for clock times (at 10 a.m.), in for months (in June), on for floors, which are surfaces (on the third floor), and in for an enclosed container (in the shared folder). The sequence is on, at, in, on, in, so in fills 2 blanks.

pitfalls.text: Matching the verb to the noun just before it instead of the true subject: The box of expensive chocolates was stolen, not were, because the subject is box.
Applying the proximity rule to each/neither of: Neither of the plans works takes a singular verb, while Neither the plan nor the reports are ready follows the nearer subject.
Choosing the option that is the closest dictionary synonym of the clue word without plugging it back in; a synonym with the wrong grammar, collocation or connotation is a planted lure.
Picking an extreme option (always, never, all, none, must) in an inference question when the passage only makes a limited or qualified claim.
Answering from real-world knowledge: an option can be true in reality and still be wrong because the passage does not state or imply it.
Treating the converse of a passage rule as an inference: All X are Y does not give All Y are X, and Some X are Y says nothing about the X that are not Y.
Choosing a or an by the first letter rather than the first sound: a university and a European, but an hour and an honest man.
Using less with countable nouns (less errors) or would have in an if-clause (If I would have known); write fewer errors and If I had known.

revisionCard.heading: Grammar rules
lines: Each/every/one of/neither of = singular verb; either…or, neither…nor = nearer subject
Strip of-phrases to find the true subject before choosing the verb
If + V1, will; If + past, would; If + had V3, would have V3
Fewer for countable, less for uncountable; in year/month, on day/date, at time
a/an by first sound: a university, an hour; the for specific, superlative, unique

revisionCard.heading: Vocabulary and blanks
lines: Clue phrase, then polarity, then plug in and test grammar
Contrast words (despite, however, yet) flip polarity; therefore and hence keep it
Roots: mal- bad, bene- good, dict- speak; check malleable-type false friends
Analogy: write the first pair's relation as a sentence, then test each option

revisionCard.heading: Reading and sequencing
lines: Skim first and last sentences, scan for question keywords, read around them
Tone from loaded adjectives; main idea neither too narrow nor too broad
Inference = strictly from the text: no extremes, no outside facts, no converse
Jumbled: opener has no pronoun or connector; fix pronoun and connector pairs

errata.claim: Indefinite pronouns such as each, every, neither and either always take singular verbs.
errata.correction: This holds when neither or either stands alone as the subject (Neither of the plans works). In the correlative pairs either…or and neither…nor the verb agrees with the nearer subject, so Neither the manager nor the employees are aware is correct, a rule stated elsewhere in the same material. Every is a determiner, not a pronoun.

errata.claim: The present perfect describes an action completed recently (I have coded).
errata.correction: The present perfect links a past action or state to the present and need not be recent or completed: I have visited Paris twice (any time up to now) and I have lived here for ten years (still continuing) are both present perfect.

errata.claim: In The committee was ___ in its decision to reject the proposal, the singular its decision rules out divided, so the answer is unanimous.
errata.correction: A singular collective noun with its is fully compatible with divided: The court was divided in its decision is standard English for a split vote. The sentence as given does not fix one answer; it needs a clue such as every member voted to reject it before unanimous is the only correct option.
